text: The NHK Broadcasting Center (NHK放送センター, Enueichikei Hōsō Sentā), the headquarters of NHK, is situated in Jinnan, Shibuya, Tokyo, Japan. It includes studios, offices, shops, and Studio Park, a popular attraction for schoolchildren and tourists. Within the same complex is the NHK Hall, where performances are regularly held and often televised. The center hosts offices of international broadcasters, including KBS of South Korea, China Central Television, the Public Broadcasting Service, and the Australian Broadcasting Corporation. Several NHK-related companies have offices in nearby buildings. The NHK Metropolitan Bureau [ja] is located here, managing the main Kanto region feeds of NHK's radio and television services. Most nationwide network programs are produced and transmitted at this center, and it serves as a base for block broadcasting in the Kanto-Koshinetsu region. Satellite broadcasting stations conduct satellite broadcasting, and international broadcasting stations, such as NHK World TV and NHK World Radio Japan, carry out international broadcasting outside Japan. The Shibuya Broadcasting Center, also the headquarters of the Japan Broadcasting Corporation, is the oldest facility in the complex, having been completed in 1965. Construction of the second building began after the East Building and was completed in 1968. The most conspicuous building in the NHK Broadcasting Center was completed in 1972, after which the functions of the Tokyo Broadcasting Center (Former Headquarters) were transferred. The NHK Hall (Japanese: NHK ホール) is a multipurpose hall in Shibuya Ward, Tokyo, designed by Nikken Sekkei (日建設計), completed in November 1972, and began operations on June 20, 1973. It is the second generation of the NHK Hall, with the first located in the NHK Tokyo Broadcasting Center; it is operated by the NHK Service Center, an affiliated corporation of NHK, and is also the home of the NHK Symphony Orchestra. The building was completed in 1988. The geographic coordinates are 35°39′53″N 139°41′45″E / 35.66474°N 139.69594°E / 35.66474; 139.69594. On August 30, 2016, the Japan Broadcasting Corporation announced a basic plan for rebuilding the broadcasting center. Construction is scheduled to begin in September 2020, with the first phase (information building) completed in 2025, marking the 100th anniversary of the start of broadcasting. The second phase (production/office building and public building) will follow, and the entire reconstruction will be completed in 2036. The estimated construction cost for the buildings (excluding broadcasting equipment) is 170 billion yen.
